\chapter*{Glossary}
\addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{Glossary}
\markboth{Glossary}{Glossary}

This glossary collects every word and phrase taught in the book. Pronunciation appears when it differs from the written form; chapter numbers show where each entry is introduced.

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{abajo}\par
\small down, below, downstairs — Late Latin bassus, low; English base, bass, abase and debase are the same lowness\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 341.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{abrir}\par
\small to open — a regular -ir verb with one irregular part, the participle abierto\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 166.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{acaso}\par
\small perhaps, by chance — a + caso, and Latin casus was a fall; English case, casual, casualty, cadence and accident are all falls too\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 324.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{además}\par
\small furthermore, moreover\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 273.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{adiós}\par
\small goodbye\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 12.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ahí · allí}\par
\small there, over there — the two places aquí has been missing, and they line up exactly with the three pointing words\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 251.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ahora}\par
\small now — the time word mañana has been waiting for, and a Latin hour in disguise\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 252.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ajeno}\par
\small somebody else's — Latin alienus from alius, other; English alien, alias and alibi all point at somebody who is not you\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 350.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{al}\par
\small to the — one of only two places where Spanish forces two words into one, and it does it because the two vowels refuse to sit next to each other\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 230.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{algo}\par
\small something — Latin aliquod, ali- plus quod, \textquotedblleft{}some other what\textquotedblright{}; the same ali- is in alias, alien and altruism\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 317.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{alguien}\par
\small somebody — Latin aliquem, ali- plus quem, \textquotedblleft{}some other whom\textquotedblright{}; algo's exact partner, built for people\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 317.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{alrededor}\par
\small around, round about — al plus rededor, from Latin retro backwards crossed with rota, a wheel; English rotate, rotund and retro all roll here\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 347.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{alto}\par
\small high, tall — Latin altus, which meant high and also deep; altitude, exalt, enhance, haughty and the oboe are all still measuring height\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 365.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{amable}\par
\small kind — Latin amabilis, loveable: the person it is easy to be fond of\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 283.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{amarillo}\par
\small yellow — from \textquotedblleft{}a little bitter,\textquotedblright{} not from any Latin word for yellow at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 151.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ambos}\par
\small both — Latin ambo, the two together; English ambidextrous, ambiguous and amphitheatre all carry the same both\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 351.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ancho}\par
\small wide — Latin amplus, spacious; ample, amplify and amplitude are the borrowed branch, and Spanish amplio is the same adjective taken fresh from the page\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 365.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{anoche}\par
\small last night — Latin ad noctem, toward night, worn into one word; the same noctem gives English nocturnal and equinox\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 322.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{antes}\par
\small before — Latin ante; English ante-, antique, ancient and ancestor all come off it, and an ancestor is one who went before\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 323.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{apenas}\par
\small barely, hardly, scarcely — a + penas, from Latin poena, a penalty; English pain, penalty, penal and subpoena are the same root\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 328.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{aquel}\par
\small that one over there, away from us both — and the second life of the word that became el in your very first chapter\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 223.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{arriba}\par
\small up, above, upstairs — Latin ripa, a riverbank; English river, riparian and arrive all come off the same bank\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 341.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{así}\par
\small thus, like this, that way — Latin ad sic, to thus; the same sic that Spanish turned into sí and that English still writes inside a quotation\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 328.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{así que}\par
\small thus, in that way — and with que after it, \textquotedblleft{}so\textquotedblright{}; built on the same sīc that gave you sí\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 175.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{asonancia}\par
\small assonance — the rhyme Spanish verse actually uses\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 276.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{aunque}\par
\small although, even though\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 270.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ayer}\par
\small yesterday\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 103.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ayudar}\par
\small to help — literally the same word as English \textquotedblleft{}aid\textquotedblright{}, arriving by a different road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 161.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{azul}\par
\small blue — an Arabic loan that became the plain everyday word, where French's cousin stayed poetic\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 139.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{bastante}\par
\small enough, quite — an ending you already decode, on a verb meaning to suffice, giving a word that means exactly \textquotedblleft{}sufficing\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 227.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{beber}\par
\small to drink (another -er verb — cementing the pattern)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 36.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{bien}\par
\small well / good / fine\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 1.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{bienvenido}\par
\small welcome — bien plus venido, well come, two pieces you already own\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 282.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{billete}\par
\small ticket\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 268.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{buenas noches}\par
\small good evening / good night\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 2.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{buenas tardes}\par
\small good afternoon\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 2.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{buenos días}\par
\small good morning (literally \textquotedblleft{}good days\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 1.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cada}\par
\small each, every — Greek kata, down or by, through Latin cata; English catalogue, catastrophe and cathedral all begin with the same kata\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 345.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{café}\par
\small coffee / a café — one useful noun before the polite request that follows\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 14.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{caminar}\par
\small to walk — built on a Celtic word for a path, beside andar, whose own past is unsettled\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 165.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cansado}\par
\small tired — a state, not a quality, which is why it takes estar and never ser\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 59.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{casi}\par
\small almost, nearly — Latin quasi, as if; English borrowed quasi whole and still hyphenates it onto anything that is nearly a thing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 328.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cerca}\par
\small near, nearby — Latin circa, around; English circa, circle, circuit and circus all turn on the same ring\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 340.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cero}\par
\small zero — Arabic sifr, empty; English took the same word twice, as zero and as cipher\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 344.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cerrar}\par
\small to close — from the bar dropped across a door, not from the Latin verb English inherited\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 166.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cien}\par
\small a hundred — Latin centum, cut short before a noun; English cent, century and percent keep the Latin, and English hundred is the very same ancient word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 351.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cierto}\par
\small true — Latin certus, sifted: what is left after you separate it out\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 284.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{comer}\par
\small to eat — your first -er verb, and the family whose yo-form you already own\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 34.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cometer un error}\par
\small to make a mistake — with the verb Spanish insists on\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 275.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{comí}\par
\small the regular singular -er preterite — comí, comiste, comió\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 104.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cómo}\par
\small how — a whole Latin phrase, quo modo, worn smooth into one word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 6.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{comprar}\par
\small to buy — from Latin's \textquotedblleft{}get ready, procure\textquotedblright{}, and not from the verb behind English compare\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 174.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{con permiso}\par
\small excuse me, said when you pass — per plus mittere, to let through\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 283.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{conmigo · contigo}\par
\small with me, with you — two words carrying the same preposition twice, because the first one stopped being audible\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 247.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{conocer}\par
\small to meet, to be acquainted with — a verb built out of the moment knowing begins\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 171.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{conseguir}\par
\small to get, to obtain — getting as following a thing until you have it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 169.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{contar}\par
\small to tell a story — and also to count, because in Spanish, as once in English, a story is something you reckon up\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 167.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{contento}\par
\small happy, content — Latin contentus, held together, from continere\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 304.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{contestar}\par
\small to answer — a Roman courtroom word that English turned into a fight and Spanish turned into a reply\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 174.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{correr}\par
\small to run — a plain -er verb sitting on one of the largest roots English ever borrowed\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 165.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{corto}\par
\small short — Latin curtus, cut off or docked; curt and curtail descend from it and cortar is its Spanish verb, while English short, shirt and skirt are Germanic and meet it only far back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 365.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{creer}\par
\small to believe, to think — putting your heart somewhere, where pensar weighs it up\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 175.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cual}\par
\small which, as, of what kind — Latin qualis, of what kind; English quality is qualitas, the what-kind-ness of a thing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 329.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{cuando}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{} — the word that puts a scene and an event in one sentence, so the two pasts can be seen doing different jobs\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 112.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{de acuerdo}\par
\small agreed — from cor, the heart: an agreement is two hearts brought together\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 284.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{de nada}\par
\small you're welcome (literally \textquotedblleft{}of nothing\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 7.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{de repente}\par
\small suddenly — Latin repente, from repens sudden, which is the present participle of repere to creep; the English reptile is the same creeping\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 356.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{deber}\par
\small should, ought to — and to owe, because the word is literally \textquotedblleft{}to have something from someone\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 175.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{deber de}\par
\small must — the guess, not the obligation\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 275.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{débil}\par
\small weak — Latin debilis; English debilitate and debility are the same word, and the written accent is there because the word ends in -l\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 327.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{decir}\par
\small to say or tell — with the singular present forms digo, dices, and dice\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 70.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{del}\par
\small of the, from the — the second and last of Spanish's forced contractions, which means once you have these two you have all of them\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 231.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{delante}\par
\small in front, ahead — Latin ante, before; English ante, antecedent, anterior, antique and anticipate all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 341.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{delgado / flaco}\par
\small thin — the kind word and the blunt one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 275.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{dentro}\par
\small inside, within — Latin de intro, from within, on intra; English interior, internal, entrance and the intro of anything share it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 341.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{depende}\par
\small it depends\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 210.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{desde}\par
\small from, since — three Latin prepositions welded shut, de plus ex plus de; despues is built the same way, out of de plus ex plus post\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 356.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{despierto}\par
\small awake — from despertar, and Latin expergisci, to set out from sleep; the e breaks to ie exactly where the stress lands\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 327.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{después}\par
\small after — Latin de ex post, three little words run together; the post in it is English postpone, postscript and posterior\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 323.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{detrás}\par
\small behind, at the back — Latin trans, across or beyond; English transfer, transit, translate and transparent all carry it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 341.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{día}\par
\small day (el día — masculine)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 1.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{dieciséis — diecinueve}\par
\small 16-19 — not words to memorise but a formula, diez y X, with the seam still visible\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 149.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{disculpe}\par
\small excuse me — from culpa, fault: literally, take the fault off me\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 283.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{distinto}\par
\small a different one — Latin distinctus, pricked apart, from dis and stinguere; English distinct, distinguish and instinct all come off the same pricking\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 350.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{doble}\par
\small double, twice as much — Latin duplus, from duo two and -plus fold; English double, duplicate, duplex and duplicity are the same two folds\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 344.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{dónde}\par
\small where?\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 36.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{dormido}\par
\small asleep — the past participle of dormir, from Latin dormire; English dormitory, dormant and dormouse are all sleeping\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 327.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{dormir}\par
\small to sleep — and the other half of the boot, where a stressed o breaks to ue\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 165.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{durante}\par
\small for, during\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 269.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{e $\to$ ie and o $\to$ ue}\par
\small comparing the two vowel changes inside the learned singular forms\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 69.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el / la}\par
\small the (masculine / feminine)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 1.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el abrazo}\par
\small a hug — from bracchium, the arm: the word says what the body does\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 282.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el abuelo}\par
\small the grandfather --- Latin avus, the root inside English avuncular and atavistic\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 306.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el aceite}\par
\small oil — Andalusi Arabic az-zayt, the oil, borrowed with its article fused on; Latin oleum gave English oil, olive, petroleum and linoleum, and the two words meet in aceite de oliva\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 361.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el agua}\par
\small water — a word that barely changed from Latin, and takes el without ever stopping being feminine\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 143.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el aire}\par
\small air — Greek aer into Latin aer into Spanish; aerial, aerobic and aerosol are the family, and malaria is Italian mala aria, bad air, a discarded medical theory frozen inside a word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 362.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el ajo}\par
\small the garlic — Latin allium, which English kept as the botanical name; aioli is this word and oil, run together\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 297.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el amanecer}\par
\small the daybreak — Latin mane, in the morning, the same piece that sits inside mañana\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 289.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el aniversario}\par
\small the anniversary — Latin annus, year, plus vertere, to turn; the year turning back to the same day, and English annual, versus and reverse share the pieces\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 349.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el apellido}\par
\small the surname — from appellitare, to call on repeatedly; English appeal sits on the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 305.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el apodo}\par
\small the nickname --- from apodar, Latin putare, to prune and so to reckon; English compute, dispute, amputate\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 309.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el árbol}\par
\small tree — Latin arbor, with one of its two r sounds slid away to l\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 278.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el armario}\par
\small wardrobe, cupboard — Latin armārium from arma, which meant tools and gear rather than weapons; arms, army, armour and alarm are cousins, and French armoire is the very same room-word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 366.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el arroz}\par
\small the rice — Arabic ar-ruzz, carrying its own article; rice is the same grain by a different road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 290.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el asiento}\par
\small the seat — Latin sedere, to sit; English sedentary, session, reside and assess all sit on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 311.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el asunto}\par
\small the matter, the affair — Latin assumptus, taken up, from ad + sumere; English assume, resume, consume and presume are all takings\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 331.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el autobús}\par
\small bus — French autobus, auto(móvil) plus (omni)bus; omnibus is the Latin dative plural of omnis, for all, so bus is a case ending left standing after its own word was thrown away\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 363.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el avión}\par
\small aeroplane — Latin avis bird, but borrowed whole from French avion, coined by Clément Ader in 1875; aviation, aviator, aviary, avian, ostrich and auspices are all avis, and el aviso is not\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 363.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el aviso}\par
\small the notice, the warning — from avisar, and Latin ad visum, to what is seen; English advise, advice, vision, evident and provide share the root videre\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 332.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el banco}\par
\small bank — a Germanic word for a bench; the money-changers of medieval Italy worked at a bench, and a broken bench, banca rotta, is English bankrupt\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 353.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el baño}\par
\small the bathroom — Latin balneum from Greek balaneion; English bath only looks related, and is not\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 310.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el barco}\par
\small ship — Late Latin barca, a small boat attested around 400 AD; barge, bark the sailing ship, embark and disembark are the same word, and the three English barks have three separate origins\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 363.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el barrio}\par
\small the neighbourhood — Andalusi Arabic barri, of the outside, from barr, the open land beyond the walls; English borrowed barrio whole\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 325.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el bebé}\par
\small the baby --- French bebe, echoic babble, the same kind of word as English baby and babble\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 309.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el boleto}\par
\small the ticket — a little bulla, a Latin seal; the same seal gives English bulletin and the papal bull\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 313.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el bosque}\par
\small the wood — a Germanic word, not a Latin one; bush, bosky and ambush are its English cousins\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 291.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el botón}\par
\small button — Old French boton, a thing that pushes out, from bouter, to thrust, taken from Germanic botan, to strike; button, buttress, rebut, abut and the butting of a goat all still push, and beat is the inherited cousin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 360.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el brazo}\par
\small the arm — Greek brakhion, \textquotedblleft{}the shorter one\textquotedblright{}, taken into Latin as bracchium; an embrace and a bracelet are both built on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 314.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el burro}\par
\small the donkey — Latin burricus, a little reddish horse, from burrus, red; English borrowed the whole word back, and the burrito with it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 296.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el caballo}\par
\small the horse — Latin caballus, the working nag, which beat the noble equus and left cavalry and chivalry behind it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 296.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el calendario}\par
\small the calendar — Latin calendarium, an account book, from calendae the first of the month when debts fell due; English calendar and intercalate share it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 343.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el calor}\par
\small heat — Latin calor from calere, to be warm; English calorie, cauldron, scald, chowder and nonchalant are all built on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 334.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cambio}\par
\small the change — Latin cambiare, borrowed from Gaulish; English change and exchange are the same word, and so is the coin you get back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 313.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el camino}\par
\small the road, the way — Late Latin camminus, borrowed from Gaulish; one of the few Celtic words Spanish kept, and the source of French chemin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 330.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el campo}\par
\small the field, the countryside — Latin campus, flat open ground; camp, campus, campaign and champion are all fought or pitched on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 299.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el centro}\par
\small centre, downtown — Latin centrum from Greek kentron, the spike a compass turns on; English centre, central, concentrate and eccentric all turn on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 347.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el chico}\par
\small the boy, the lad --- Latin ciccum, a worthless trifle; a word that means small first and boy second\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 308.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cielo}\par
\small the sky — Latin caelum, which is also the ceiling over a room and the cerulean of a paint box\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 289.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cine}\par
\small cinema — short for cinematografo, Greek kinema movement plus graphein to write, a movement-writer; the same kinein is in English kinetic\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 354.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el coche}\par
\small car — Hungarian kocsi, a cart from the town of Kocs, by way of German Kutsche and French coche; English coach is the same word, and the coach on the touchline began as a tutor who carried a student through\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 363.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cocinero}\par
\small the cook — coquere, to cook; the kitchen, the biscuit and a precocious child are all in it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 285.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el color}\par
\small colour — Latin color, from celare to hide, because a colour is what covers a thing; conceal, cell, occult and even hell are the same hiding\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 358.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el conjunto}\par
\small the set, the whole group — Latin coniunctus, yoked together, from com and iungere; English junction, join and even yoga come off the same yoking\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 352.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el consejo}\par
\small advice, and also a council — Latin consilium; English counsel and council are the same word that stopped being one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 321.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el corazón}\par
\small heart — Latin cor, cordis with a Spanish augmentative ending; cordial, courage, accord and discord are all hearts, and record is literally to bring a thing back to the heart\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 364.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cuarto}\par
\small the quarter, a fourth — Latin quartus, fourth, on quattuor four; English quarter, quart, quartet and quarantine all count to four\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 342.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cuchillo}\par
\small the knife — Latin cultellus, a little culter; cutlery, cutlass and the plough's coulter are the same blade\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 294.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cuello}\par
\small the neck — Latin collum, which is also the collar round it and the accolade thrown round it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 293.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el cuidado}\par
\small care, caution — Latin cogitatum, a thing thought about, from cogitare to think; English cogitate and Descartes' cogito are the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 333.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el dedo}\par
\small finger, and equally toe — Latin digitus; digit became a numeral because people count on fingers, and digital reached the computer through the numerals rather than through the hand\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 364.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el descanso}\par
\small the rest — des- undoes cansar, to tire; rest in Spanish is defined as the reversal of being worn down\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 315.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el diente}\par
\small the tooth — Latin dentem, with the e broken to ie; a dandelion is a dent de lion, a lion's tooth\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 314.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el dinero}\par
\small money — the name of a Roman coin, still doing service two thousand years later\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 280.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el dolor}\par
\small the pain — Latin dolor; condolence hurts with you, and indolent once felt no pain at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 286.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el esposo}\par
\small the husband --- Latin spondere, to pledge solemnly; English spouse, sponsor, respond, despondent\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 306.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el faro}\par
\small the lighthouse — named after Pharos, the island at Alexandria that held the first one; a place name that became the word for the thing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 302.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el favor}\par
\small a favour, a good turn — Latin favere, to be well disposed toward somebody; English favour, favourite and favourable are all the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 320.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el fin}\par
\small the end — Latin finis, a boundary stone between fields; English final, finish, finite, define and confine all mark the same edge\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 348.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el fondo}\par
\small the bottom, the back of a room — Latin fundus, the bottom of a thing; English found, foundation, fund and profound all sit on it, and Spanish hondo is the same word with f turned to h\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 355.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el frío}\par
\small cold — Latin frigidus; English frigid, refrigerate and refrigerator are the same word, and hace frio has been carrying this noun all along\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 334.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el fuego}\par
\small fire — Latin focus, which meant the hearth and not the fire at all; focus, focal, curfew and fuel all come down from that hearth, while the Latin word for fire itself lost the fight across Romance\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 362.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el ganado}\par
\small the livestock — from ganar, to gain: cattle are simply \textquotedblleft{}what has been gained\textquotedblright{}, the way English cattle and chattel are what you own\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 299.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el gramo}\par
\small a gram — Greek gramma, a written thing and also a small weight, from graphein to scratch; grammar, program, diagram and telegram are the same gramma\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 359.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hambre}\par
\small hunger — Latin famen from fames; a feminine noun that takes el before its stressed a-, and one of the f-to-h words like hacer, hijo and hierro\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 334.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hermano, la hermana}\par
\small brother and sister — NOT from frater/soror, but from an adjective meaning \textquotedblleft{}of the same seed\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 140.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hijo}\par
\small the son --- Latin filius, cousin to English filial and affiliate; the f- that became a silent h-\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 306.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hilo}\par
\small the thread — Latin filum with its f worn down to a silent h; filament, filigree and a file of soldiers are all threads\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 301.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hombro}\par
\small the shoulder — Latin umerus, which doctors still call the humerus; the h is silent and came late\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 293.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el horario}\par
\small the timetable, the opening hours — Latin horarium, on hora an hour; English hour, horoscope and horology come off the same root, and the -ario ending is English -ary\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 342.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el horno}\par
\small the oven — Latin furnus, wearing the silent h that marks where an f used to stand; furnace is the same fire\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 297.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hospital}\par
\small hospital — Latin hospitale, a house kept for guests, from hospes, which meant the host and the guest at once; English host, hotel, hostel and hospitality all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 353.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el hotel}\par
\small hotel — French hotel, from Old French hostel, from the same Latin hospitale as hospital; the little hat on the French o is a headstone for a lost s\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 354.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el huevo}\par
\small egg — Latin ovum, wearing an h that exists only to help your eyes\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 280.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el instante}\par
\small the instant — Latin instans, standing upon you, from in plus stare; English instant, instance and constant all stand on the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 348.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el invitado}\par
\small a guest — the invited one; Spanish names the person by what was done to him\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 282.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el jabón}\par
\small soap — Latin sapo, which Latin had itself borrowed from its northern neighbours\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 287.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el jardín}\par
\small garden — Frankish gardo, an enclosure, the same Germanic word English kept as yard and borrowed back from French as garden; kindergarten is a children's enclosure\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 354.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el kilo}\par
\small a kilo — Greek khilioi, a thousand; it is not Latin mille, so kilo and the mil of mil gracias are two unrelated thousands\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 359.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el lago}\par
\small the lake — Latin lacus; lake, lagoon and lacuna are all the same standing water\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 292.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el libro}\par
\small book — named after the part of a tree people wrote on before paper\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 57.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el litro}\par
\small a litre — Greek litra, a Sicilian unit, the same word Latin took as libra, the pound; a pound is still abbreviated lb, and Libra is the scales in the sky\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 359.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el llanto}\par
\small the weeping — Latin planctus, a beating; Roman mourners struck their own chest, and pl- became ll- on the way into Spanish\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 316.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el lugar}\par
\small the place, the spot — Latin locus through localis; the same locus is already inside hasta luego and en primer lugar\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 325.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el maestro}\par
\small the teacher — magister, from magis, more; and minister, from minus, less\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 285.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el mapa}\par
\small the map — Latin mappa, a cloth; the world was drawn on a napkin, and napkin is the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 312.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el mar}\par
\small sea — Latin mare; marine, maritime, marina and ultramarine are borrowed from it, while the mer- of mermaid and the words marsh and moor are inherited English cousins of the same ancient root\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 362.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el mercado}\par
\small market — Latin mercatus from merx, goods; English market, merchant, commerce and even mercy grow out of the same trade\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 346.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el metro}\par
\small a metre — Greek metron, a measure, as in diameter and geometry; the underground metro is a different word, short for metropolitano, from meter a mother plus polis a city\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 359.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el miedo}\par
\small the fear — Latin metus, with the e broken to ie; meticulous once meant full of fear\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 315.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el minuto}\par
\small the minute — Latin minutus, made small, from minuere to lessen; English minute, minor, minus, diminish and minuscule are the same smallness\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 342.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el modo}\par
\small the way, the mode — Latin modus, a measure; English mode, model, modern, modest and moderate are measurings, and Spanish como is quomodo, in what measure\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 331.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el momento}\par
\small a moment — Latin momentum, the smallest movement that tips a balance\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 303.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el mundo}\par
\small the world — Latin mundus, meaning clean and orderly; English mundane is the same word, and Greek kosmos made the identical jump from order to world\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 330.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el museo}\par
\small museum — Greek mouseion, a seat of the Muses; the Mouseion at Alexandria was a place scholars lived and worked, and the same Muses are inside English music\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 353.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el niño}\par
\small the boy, the child --- a nursery word with no Latin pedigree, and the one English borrowed whole as El Niño\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 308.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el nombre}\par
\small the name — Latin nomen, cousin to English name and root of noun and nominate\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 305.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el norte}\par
\small north — Germanic northa through Old French nord; this is literally the English word north, borrowed back into a Romance language\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 347.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el número}\par
\small the number — Latin numerus; English number, numeral, numerous, enumerate and numb all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 344.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el objeto}\par
\small the object, the thing — Latin objectum, thrown before, from ob and iacere to throw; English object, project, inject, eject and subject are all throws\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 345.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el oeste}\par
\small west — Germanic westaz through Old French ouest; the same word as English west, and behind it the old root for evening that also gives vespers\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 347.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el oído}\par
\small the hearing, the inner ear — the past participle of oír made into a noun; Latin audire is under audio, audience and obedient\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 314.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el ojo}\par
\small the eye — Latin oculus; English eye is its distant cousin, not a translation of it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 286.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el padre, la madre}\par
\small father and mother — among the oldest reconstructible words in the whole family\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 140.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el país}\par
\small the country — Late Latin pagensis, of the country district, from pagus a village; English pagan and peasant are both country-dwellers\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 325.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pan}\par
\small bread — and the compañero who shares it with you\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 143.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pantalón}\par
\small trousers — French pantalon, from Pantalone, the Venetian comic stock character and his long tight legwear; English pantaloons, clipped to pants, is the very same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 360.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el papel}\par
\small the paper — from papyrus, the reed the Egyptians wrote on; it also means the part an actor plays, because the part was written on one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 301.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pariente}\par
\small the relative --- Latin parere, to give birth; English parent and postpartum, and a false friend worth knowing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 309.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el parque}\par
\small park — Frankish parrik, an enclosure, through Medieval Latin parricus; a park was a fence before it was grass, and the English dialect word paddock is the same fence\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 354.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pasaporte}\par
\small the passport — pass plus port; the paper that lets you through the gate, from Latin passus and porta\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 313.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pastor}\par
\small the shepherd — from pascere, to graze; the pasture, the pastor of a church and a repast are all feeding\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 299.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pecho}\par
\small the chest — Latin pectus, whose ct became ch on the same road that took noctem to noche; English keeps the Latin in pectoral\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 315.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el permiso}\par
\small permission, leave — Latin permissus from permittere, per + mittere, to let go through; English permit, mission, transmit, submit and promise are all sendings\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 332.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pescado}\par
\small fish as food — Latin piscātus, the catch, from piscārī to fish, on piscis; Pisces and piscine are borrowed, English fish is the inherited cousin, and pecado sin is a different word entirely\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 361.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el peso}\par
\small weight — Latin pensum, a thing weighed out, from pendere to weigh and to hang; pension, spend, expensive, pendant and ponder are all still weighing something\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 359.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pie}\par
\small the foot — Latin pedem, from a root so old that Hindi pair, Persian pa and English foot are all the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 314.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el piso}\par
\small floor, storey, flat — from pisar, to tread, from Late Latin pinsare to pound; English pestle and piston are the same pounding, and in Spain un piso is a flat\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 355.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el placer}\par
\small pleasure — Latin placere, to please; English please, placid, plea and placebo are all the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 321.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el plato}\par
\small a plate — Greek platys, flat: the same flatness in a plaza and in a platypus\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 287.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el precio}\par
\small the price — Latin pretium, worth; English price, precious, appreciate and praise all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 311.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el primo}\par
\small the cousin --- Latin primus, first; the same root as primero, and as English prime and primary\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 307.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el principio}\par
\small the beginning — Latin principium from princeps, the one who takes first place; English prince, principal and principle are the same first taking\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 348.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el pueblo}\par
\small the village, and also the people — Latin populus, which gave popular, population and public\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 292.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el puente}\par
\small the bridge — Latin pontem; a pontoon floats one and a pontiff is, underneath, a bridge-builder\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 295.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el puerto}\par
\small the harbour — Latin portus, the twin of the porta you already have; import, export and opportunity are all ships coming in\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 302.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el punto}\par
\small the point, the dot — Latin punctum, a prick, from pungere to prick; English point, puncture, punctual, punctuation and pungent share the needle\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 342.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el queso}\par
\small cheese — Latin caseus, the very same word as English cheese by another road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 280.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el rato}\par
\small a while, a short time — Latin raptus, a snatching, from rapere to seize; English rapid, rapt, rapture and ravish are all seizures\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 331.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el regalo}\par
\small a present — from regalar, French regaler, on Old French gale, merry-making; English gala and to regale a guest are the same fun, and it has nothing to do with king or regal\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 357.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el reloj}\par
\small the clock — Greek horologium, the hour-teller; the same hora sits in English hour and horoscope\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 312.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el remedio}\par
\small the remedy — re- and mederi, to heal again; medicine, medical and a medic are all the same healing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 300.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el respeto}\par
\small respect — Latin respicere, to look back at somebody; the same specere gives English spectacle, inspect and suspect\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 321.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el restaurante}\par
\small restaurant — French restaurant, a thing that restores, from Latin restaurare; the first restaurant was a broth sold to people who felt weak, and the room took the name of the soup\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 354.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el resto}\par
\small the rest, what is left — Latin restare, to stand back, from re and stare; English rest and arrest stand on the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 352.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el rincón}\par
\small the inside corner of a room — Arabic rukn, a corner or a supporting pillar; the street corner, la esquina, is Latin, so Spanish gets its two corners from two languages\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 355.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el ruido}\par
\small the noise — Latin rugitus, a roaring, from rugire to roar; the same root gave English rut, the roaring season of deer\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 333.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el saludo}\par
\small a greeting — from salutem, health: to greet was to wish someone their health\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 282.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el sendero}\par
\small the path — Latin semita, a by-way, with semi- meaning half: a path is a half-road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 295.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el siglo}\par
\small the century, the age — Latin saeculum, a generation or a lifetime; English secular is the same word, meaning of this age rather than of eternity\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 343.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el silencio}\par
\small the silence — Latin silentium from silere, to be still; English silence, silent and the silent film all come off it unchanged\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 333.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el sueño}\par
\small the sleep, and the dream — Latin somnus with the o broken to ue; insomnia and somnolent keep the o intact\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 300.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el sur}\par
\small south — Germanic sunthaz through Old French sud; the same word as English south, and probably built on the word for sun\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 347.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tamaño}\par
\small size — Latin tam magnum, so big, welded shut; the tam is the tan inside tambien and tampoco, and magnus is the magn- of magnify and magnitude\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 358.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el techo}\par
\small roof, ceiling — Latin tectum, the covered part, from tegere to cover; to protect is to cover in front, to detect is to take the cover off, and a Roman toga was a covering\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 355.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el teléfono}\par
\small the telephone — Greek tele far plus phone voice; a far-voice, and both halves are everywhere in English\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 312.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tenedor}\par
\small the fork — built on tener, to hold: it is \textquotedblleft{}the holder\textquotedblright{}, the same shape as any Spanish word ending in -dor\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 297.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tiempo}\par
\small the one noun that covers both \textquotedblleft{}time\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{} — because Latin tempus already did\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 148.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tío}\par
\small the uncle --- Greek theios, borrowed into Late Latin; the word English did not take, because English took avunculus instead\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 307.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tipo}\par
\small the kind, the sort — Greek typos, a blow and the dent a blow leaves; English type, typical, typography and prototype all take the same impression\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 350.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tobillo}\par
\small the ankle — from Latin tuber, a swelling; a tuber in the ground and a protuberance are the same lump\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 293.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tomate}\par
\small the tomato — Nahuatl tomatl, one of the words Spanish carried back across the Atlantic\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 290.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el trigo}\par
\small the wheat — Latin triticum, the rubbed grain, from terere, to rub; trite is worn down the same way\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 290.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el triple}\par
\small triple, three times as much — Latin triplus, three plus the -plus that means fold; English triple, treble and triplicate are all three folds\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 351.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el tronco}\par
\small the trunk — Latin truncus, meaning lopped or maimed; to truncate is to do it on purpose\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 291.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el turno}\par
\small the turn, your slot — Greek tornos, a lathe, through Latin tornus; English turn, tour, tournament, contour and tornado all spin off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 348.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el valle}\par
\small the valley — Latin vallis; valley, vale and avalanche all come down the same slope\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 292.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el vaso}\par
\small a glass — Latin vas, a vessel: named for what it does, not for what it is made of\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 287.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el vecino}\par
\small the neighbour — from vicus, a village street: the person off your own block\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 285.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el vestido}\par
\small dress — Latin vestire, to clothe, its past participle standing alone as a noun; vest, invest, divest and travesty are all still clothing something, and wear is the inherited cousin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 360.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el viaje}\par
\small the journey — Latin viaticum, the provisions you packed for the road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 288.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el viento}\par
\small wind — Latin ventus, and the English word that is its cousin rather than its borrowing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 278.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el vino}\par
\small wine — one Latin root that reached English by three separate roads, plus one English built at home\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 143.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{el zapato}\par
\small shoe — origin genuinely unknown; Portuguese sapato, Catalan sabata, French savate, Italian ciabatta and Arabic sabbat all share it, and the famous sabotage story attached to it is false\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 360.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{en efecto}\par
\small indeed — from ex and facere, carried out; it confirms what somebody has just said, and does not mean \textquotedblleft{}in effect\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 298.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{en mi opinión}\par
\small in my opinion\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 270.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{en primer lugar}\par
\small in the first place, firstly\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 273.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{en resumen}\par
\small in short — and the last thing this book asks of you\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 277.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{encantado}\par
\small delighted to meet you — Latin incantare, to sing a spell into; English enchanted\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 305.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{enfermo}\par
\small ill — Latin infirmus, not firm; the same word as English infirm\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 304.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{enfrente}\par
\small opposite, across from, facing — Latin frontem, the forehead; English front, frontier, affront, confront and effrontery all come off the same brow\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 340.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{enseguida}\par
\small right away — en seguida, \textquotedblleft{}in what follows,\textquotedblright{} from Latin sequi, to follow; English sequence, sequel and pursue come off the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 322.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{entender}\par
\small to understand — literally \textquotedblleft{}to stretch toward\textquotedblright{}; the second e$\to$ie stem-changer\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 154.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{entero}\par
\small whole, entire — Latin integer, untouched, from in not plus tangere to touch; English integer, integrity and intact are the same untouched thing\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 352.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{entonces}\par
\small then — Latin in tunc, \textquotedblleft{}at that time\textquotedblright{}; tunc and English then both grow out of the old pointing word that also gives the, that and there\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 323.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{es decir}\par
\small that is to say — the same idea in your own words\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 277.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{es que…}\par
\small it's just that…\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 272.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{escaso}\par
\small scarce, in short supply — Vulgar Latin excarpsus, picked over, from ex and carpere to pluck; English scarce, excerpt and carpet are the same plucking\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 352.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{escribir}\par
\small to write — from a Latin verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to scratch\textquotedblright{}, and the reason Spanish puts an e- in front\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 156.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ese}\par
\small that one, by you — the slot Latin's iste left empty when Spanish moved it, filled by a word that used to mean self\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 222.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{español}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}Spanish\textquotedblright{} — the language, the people, and the Roman name for the peninsula underneath it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 22.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{esperar}\par
\small to wait — and to hope, and to expect, all in one verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 174.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{espero viajar}\par
\small I hope to travel\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 269.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{está en…}\par
\small is in or at… — locate someone with estar and the already-known en\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 48.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{estar}\par
\small to be — but the \emph{standing} kind, straight from Latin stāre\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 8.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{estás / está}\par
\small what estar is for — a current state or location — and the only two forms you need this chapter\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 8.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{este}\par
\small this one, here, next to me — the first of three words for pointing, and the reason Spanish never needs to say \textquotedblleft{}the this book\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 221.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{estudiante}\par
\small student — a word you can build yourself, out of a verb you already have\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 52.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{estudiar}\par
\small to study (a third -ar verb — the pattern is automatic now)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 21.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{exacto}\par
\small exactly — from exigere, to drive out, and then to weigh out precisely\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 284.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{explicar}\par
\small to explain — literally to unfold, and the verb that names what this whole chapter has been building\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 175.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{falso}\par
\small false, fake — Latin falsus, the past participle of fallere, to trip somebody up; English fail, fault, fallacy and false all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 324.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{feliz}\par
\small happy\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 269.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{fuerte}\par
\small strong, loud — Latin fortis, the same root already spent on la fuerza; English fort, force, effort, comfort and fortify all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 327.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{fui}\par
\small the shared singular preterite of ser and ir — fui, fuiste, fue\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 103.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{gato}\par
\small cat — a word that travelled out of Africa with the animal, pushing Latin's own fēlēs aside\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 150.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{gracias}\par
\small thank you\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 7.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{grande}\par
\small big — the first word in this book for what something is like, and it does not change for gender\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 58.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{gustar}\par
\small to please — the verb English calls \textquotedblleft{}to like\textquotedblright{}, built the other way round\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 163.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{habitación}\par
\small room\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 268.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hablar}\par
\small to speak / to talk — at root, \textquotedblleft{}to tell stories\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 16.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hablaré}\par
\small I will speak\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 49.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{Hablo español}\par
\small your first sentence built from parts — and the rule that languages take no article\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 22.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hace calor, hace frío, hace sol}\par
\small the three weather words Spanish reports with hacer — \textquotedblleft{}it makes heat,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it makes cold,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it makes sun\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 148.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hacer}\par
\small to do or make — with the singular present forms hago, haces, and hace\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 70.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hasta}\par
\small until / up to\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 12.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hasta luego}\par
\small see you later (literally \textquotedblleft{}until later\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 13.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hasta mañana}\par
\small see you tomorrow (literally \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 13.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hasta pronto}\par
\small see you soon (literally \textquotedblleft{}until soon\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 13.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hay}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}there are\textquotedblright{} — one word for both, which no other Spanish verb form manages\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 191.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hola}\par
\small hello / hi\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 1.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{hoy}\par
\small today — a whole Latin phrase worn down to three letters, and the tense it prefers\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 252.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{igual}\par
\small the same, equal — Latin aequalis from aequus, level; English equal, equator and adequate are all about a surface with no tilt in it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 350.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip
