\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{incluso}\par
\small even, including — Latin inclusus from includere, in + claudere, to shut in; English include, enclose, recluse, seclude and conclude are all shuttings\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 328.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ir}\par
\small to go — with the three singular present forms voy, vas, and va\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 49.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{jamás}\par
\small never, ever — Latin iam magis, already more; the magis half is the same word that became más, and French jamais took the identical road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 328.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{jugar}\par
\small to play — from Latin's word for joking, and the only verb in the language that breaks u to ue\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 170.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} for something feminine — the one word in this pair that never had to change\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 84.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la abuela}\par
\small the grandmother --- the avus root swung feminine, the same -o/-a switch as hijo and hija\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 306.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la agenda}\par
\small the diary, the schedule — Latin agenda, the things that must be done, from agere to drive; English agent, agile and act come off the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 349.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la aguja}\par
\small the needle — a little acus, a sharp; the same sharp that names the acute accent, and the one in acupuncture\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 301.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la almohada}\par
\small pillow — Andalusi Arabic al-mukhadda, the cheek-instrument, with the Arabic article fused on; this word has no English relative at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 366.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la amiga}\par
\small a friend, of a woman — Latin amica, from the same amare as amable\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 285.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ayuda}\par
\small help — Latin adiutare, to bring strength toward someone; the same root gives English aid\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 303.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la biblioteca}\par
\small library — Greek biblion, a book, plus theke, a chest, so a book-chest; the same theke gave Spanish bodega and botica, French boutique and English apothecary\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 353.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la bicicleta}\par
\small bicycle — French bicyclette, Latin bi- two on Greek kyklos circle, wheel; cycle, tricycle, cyclops and the 1848 coinage cyclone are the same root, English wheel is its inherited cousin, and encyclopedia comes from a misread Greek phrase\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 363.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la boca}\par
\small the mouth — Latin bucca was the cheek, and the cheek pushed the mouth out of the job\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 286.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la bolsa}\par
\small the bag — Latin bursa from Greek byrsa, a hide; English purse, bursar and reimburse are all the same leather\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 311.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cabeza}\par
\small the head — Spanish KEPT Latin's real word, unlike French, which replaced it with slang for \textquotedblleft{}pot\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 141.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la caja}\par
\small box — Latin capsa, the case a Roman kept scrolls in, probably reaching Castilian through Catalan or Occitan; case, capsule and chassis are cousins, and English cash first meant the box itself\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 366.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la calle}\par
\small the street — Latin callis, the narrow track worn through rough ground by driven animals; the town's word began in the hills\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 302.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la calma}\par
\small the calm — Late Latin cauma from Greek kauma, burning heat; the windless noon at sea gave sailors a word for stillness\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 333.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cama}\par
\small bed — one of the commonest Spanish words, and nobody has settled where it came from\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 279.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cantidad}\par
\small the quantity, the amount — Latin quantitas from quantus, how much; English quantity, quantum and quantify all ask the same question\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 351.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cara}\par
\small face — Late Latin cara, generally traced to Greek kara head though the trail is not clean; the identical cara meaning expensive is a separate root, carus, which gave English charity, caress and cherish\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 364.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la carne}\par
\small meat, flesh — Latin carō, stem carn-; carnal, incarnate and carnage are the direct cousins, and carnival is carnelevare, the removing of meat\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 361.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la carta}\par
\small the letter, and the menu — Latin charta from Greek khartes, a papyrus sheet; English chart, charter, card and cartoon are all it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 312.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la casa}\par
\small house, home — and a word French wore down so far it stopped looking like a noun\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 56.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cebolla}\par
\small the onion — Latin caepulla, a little caepa; the chive in English is the same root, undiminished\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 290.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cesta}\par
\small the basket — Latin cista from Greek kiste, a box; English chest and cistern are the same container by two different doors\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 301.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la chica}\par
\small the girl --- the same ciccum root, and the one word here that English borrowed from Spanish rather than the reverse\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 308.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cita}\par
\small an appointment, a date — from citar, Latin citare to summon, from ciere to set in motion; English cite, recite, incite and excite are all the same summons\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 356.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ciudad}\par
\small the city — Latin civitatem from civis, a citizen; English city, civic, civil, civilian and citizen are the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 325.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la clase}\par
\small a class, a kind, a lesson — Latin classis, one of the six bands Rome sorted its citizens into by wealth; a writer of the top band was classicus, which is where classic comes from\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 358.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la colina}\par
\small the hill — Latin collis, from a root meaning to rise; excel and culminate rise from the same place\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 292.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la comida}\par
\small food, a meal — a noun you can build yourself out of a verb you already own\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 77.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cosa}\par
\small the thing — Latin causa, a cause or legal case, which drifted to mean thing; English cause, because, accuse and excuse keep the original sense\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 331.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cosecha}\par
\small the harvest — from collecta, the gathered-up, which is the colligere you already took apart once\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 299.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cuchara}\par
\small a spoon — Latin cochlear, from cochlea, a snail shell you dug the snail out with\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 287.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cuenta}\par
\small the bill — Latin computare, to reckon together; English compute, count and account are the same word at three distances\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 311.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la cuerda}\par
\small the rope — Greek khorde by way of Latin chorda, a gut string; cord, chord and cordon are the same string, and the o breaks to ue again\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 301.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la culpa}\par
\small fault, blame — Latin culpa; English culprit and culpable are the same word, and mea culpa was never translated at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 320.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la década}\par
\small the decade — Greek deka, ten, through Latin decas; English decade, decimal, December and dean all count in tens\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 349.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la demora}\par
\small the delay — Latin mora, a lingering, through demorari; English demur and moratorium are the same hanging back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 348.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la derecha}\par
\small the right, the right-hand side — Latin directus, straightened, from dirigere to set straight; English direct, direction, erect and address share it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 340.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la despedida}\par
\small the farewell — from despedir, Latin expetere, to ask out: a leave-taking was a request\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 288.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la disculpa}\par
\small the apology — dis- undoing culpa, blame, from Latin culpa; English culpable, culprit, exculpate and mea culpa keep the blame in place\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 332.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la docena}\par
\small the dozen — Latin duodecim, two-ten, from duo and decem; English dozen and duodecimal are the same twelve\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 344.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ducha}\par
\small the shower — Latin ducere, to lead; the same root leads water through an aqueduct and gives English duct, conduct and duke\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 310.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la edad}\par
\small age — Latin aetatem from aetas and aevum, a lifetime; the -dad ending you know from verdad and ciudad, and English age, eternal, medieval and longevity share the root\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 334.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la enfermera}\par
\small the nurse — from infirmus, not firm: named after the patient, not the work\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 285.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la entrada}\par
\small the entrance, and the admission ticket — Latin intrare from intra, within; English enter, entrance and interior are all inside it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 313.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la época}\par
\small the age, the era, the season — Greek epokhe, a stopping point, from epekhein to hold back; English epoch is the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 343.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la escalera}\par
\small stairs, ladder — Latin scālāria from scāla, a ladder; scale, ascend, descend and echelon are cousins, while escalate arrived by way of a 1900 trademark\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 366.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la escoba}\par
\small the broom — Latin scopa, a bundle of twigs, wearing the Spanish e- step for the third time\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 294.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la escuela}\par
\small school — Latin schola from Greek skholē, spare time; English school, scholar and scholastic keep the leisure that turned into study\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 346.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la espalda}\par
\small the back — Latin spatula, a broad blade; the same blade is a spatula, a spade and an epaulette\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 293.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la esposa}\par
\small the wife --- the same spondere pledge, feminine; and the reason handcuffs are called esposas\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 307.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la esquina}\par
\small the corner — from a Germanic word for a shinbone; English shin is the same bone, and a corner is an edge as sharp as one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 302.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la estación}\par
\small station — Latin statio from stare, to stand; a station is a standing-place, and English station, stationary, statue and stable stand on the same verb\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 346.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la estrella}\par
\small the star — Latin stella, wearing the e- that Spanish puts in front of an s and a consonant\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 289.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la etapa}\par
\small a stage, a leg of a journey — French etape, once a storehouse where an army drew supplies, from Middle Dutch stapel a heap; English staple is the same pile\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 356.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la familia}\par
\small the family --- Latin familia, the whole household including its servants; English family and familiar\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 309.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la farmacia}\par
\small pharmacy, chemist's — Greek pharmakon, a drug that could cure or kill; the Greek word never chose between the remedy and the poison, and English pharmacy keeps it whole\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 353.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la fecha}\par
\small the date — Latin facta, done or made, from facere; English fact, feat, factory, affect and perfect all come off the same making\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 343.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la fiebre}\par
\small the fever — Latin febris, which English borrowed early as fever and late as febrile\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 286.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la fiesta}\par
\small the holiday, the party — Latin festa, the feast days; English feast, festival and festive are the same word, and English borrowed fiesta itself\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 349.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la flor}\par
\small flower — Latin flos, and the reason English flour is spelled so oddly\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 278.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la forma}\par
\small shape — Latin forma, which came into Spanish twice; the borrowed half is la forma, and the inherited half is hermoso, beautiful, from formosus, well shaped\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 358.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la fuerza}\par
\small the strength — Latin fortia from fortis, with the o broken to ue; force, fort, effort and comfort are all built on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 315.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la gallina}\par
\small the hen — Latin gallina, the female of gallus; and in both languages the bird is also what you call a coward\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 296.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la garganta}\par
\small the throat — a word made out of the noise itself, as gargle and gurgle are\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 286.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la gente}\par
\small people --- Latin gens, the clan; the root of English gentle, genteel, Gentile and general\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 308.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la granja}\par
\small the farm — from granum, the grain: a farm is named after the one thing it was built to store\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 299.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la hija}\par
\small the daughter --- the same filius root, swung to -a; English filial covers both\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 306.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la hora}\par
\small hour / o'clock — telling the time, and a word Spanish inherited almost unchanged from Latin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 147.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la huella}\par
\small the footprint — from hollar, to tread, and behind that fullare, to trample cloth; a fuller was the man who did it with his feet\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 302.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la iglesia}\par
\small church — Latin ecclesia from Greek ekklesia, the people called out to assemble; English ecclesiastical is the same gathering\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 346.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la isla}\par
\small the island — Latin insula; insular, isolate, peninsula and insulin all come off the same rock\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 295.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la izquierda}\par
\small the left, the left-hand side — Basque ezkerra, one of the few pre-Roman words in Spanish; it drove out Latin sinistra, which English kept as sinister\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 340.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la jornada}\par
\small the day's stretch, a working day — Latin diurnus, of the day, through Occitan; English journey, journal and adjourn are the same day\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 349.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la lámpara}\par
\small lamp — Greek lampas, a torch, from lampein, to shine; lamp and lantern are cousins, and Spanish relámpago, lightning, comes free with it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 366.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la leche}\par
\small milk — Latin lac, stem lact-; lactose and lactate are learned coinages and Italian latte is the same word, while lettuce is lactūca, named for the milky sap of a cut stem\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 361.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la llave}\par
\small the key — Latin clavis, the little key; the same root gives English clavicle, clef and conclave\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 310.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la llegada}\par
\small the arrival — from llegar, Latin plicare, to fold: a ship folded its sails and had arrived\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 288.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la luna}\par
\small moon — Latin luna, worn down from an earlier louksna, the shiny one, from the same ancient root as la luz; light is the inherited English cousin, lucid and luminous the borrowed ones, and leukemia the one that came through Greek\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 362.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la luz}\par
\small the light — Latin lux, lucem; English keeps it in lucid, translucent and elucidate\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 310.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la madrugada}\par
\small the small hours, daybreak — Latin maturus, ripe or early, through madurgar; English mature and premature are the same ripeness\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 342.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la maleta}\par
\small the suitcase — a little mala, the Gaulish word for a bag; English mail, the post, is named after the same bag\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 312.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la manera}\par
\small the way, the manner — from Latin manuarius, of the hand, and manus a hand; English manner, manual, manufacture and manage are all handlings\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 331.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la mano}\par
\small the hand — feminine despite ending in -o, Spanish's most famous gender exception\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 141.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la manta}\par
\small the blanket — Latin mantum, a cloak; the mantle, the mantelpiece and the manta ray are all cloaks\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 294.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la manzana}\par
\small apple — named after a Roman gardener whose variety outlived him\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 280.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la marca}\par
\small a mark, a brand — Germanic marka, a boundary; the border lands were marches, their lords marquises, and Latin margo, an edge, is the cousin that gives margin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 358.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la mayoría}\par
\small most of them, the majority — Latin maior, greater, from magnus; English major, mayor and magnitude are all the same greatness\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 352.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la mesa}\par
\small the table — Latin mensa, the measured board; English borrowed mesa whole for the flat-topped hill\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 310.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la miel}\par
\small the honey — Latin mel, which sweetens mellifluous, molasses and marmalade\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 290.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la mitad}\par
\small the half — Latin medietatem, the middle-ness, from medius middle; English medium, median, mediate and moiety come off it, and the -dad ending is the one you know\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 344.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la molestia}\par
\small trouble, bother — Latin molestia from moles, a heavy mass; English molecule is the same mass made small\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 320.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la moneda}\par
\small the coin — Latin moneta, a title of the goddess Juno in whose temple Rome struck its coins; English money and mint are both her\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 313.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la montaña}\par
\small the mountain — Latin mons; paramount is above the hill and an amount is what it comes to\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 292.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la mujer}\par
\small woman, and also wife — Latin mulier, whose own origin is unexplained; English took almost nothing from it beyond the rare muliebrity, while Latin homo gave human, homage and homicide\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 364.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la nariz}\par
\small nose — Latin nāris, which meant nostril and usually came in the plural nārēs; English nose is the inherited cousin, nasal the borrowed one, and meter las narices keeps the Latin plural alive\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 364.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la Navidad}\par
\small Christmas — Latin nativitatem, a birth, from nasci to be born; Spanish nada and nadie are the same verb, a born thing and born people\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 357.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la niebla}\par
\small the mist — Latin nebula, the word set aside earlier as the near-cousin of nubes; nebulous is the same mist\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 295.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la nieve}\par
\small snow — Latin nivem, and the s- that Latin dropped and English kept\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 278.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la niña}\par
\small the girl --- the counterpart of El Niño, and the reason the pupil of the eye is a little girl in both languages\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 308.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la noche}\par
\small night / evening (la noche — feminine)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 2.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la nube}\par
\small the cloud — Latin nubes, and the ancestor of nuance, which began as a shade of cloud\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 289.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ocasión}\par
\small an occasion, a chance — Latin occasio, a falling-down, from ob and cadere to fall; accident, cadence, case, chance and cascade are all that same falling\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 356.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la oficina}\par
\small office — Latin officina, a workshop, squeezed out of opificina from opus work and facere to make; English office, officer and opus are the same making\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 346.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la olla}\par
\small the pot — Latin olla, unchanged in two thousand years; potpourri is a French translation of olla podrida\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 294.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la orilla}\par
\small the shore — Latin ora, an edge or border, with the small ending: the little edge of anything\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 295.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la oveja}\par
\small the sheep — Latin ovicula, a little ovis; Spanish kept the small one and dropped the full-sized word entirely\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 296.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la paciencia}\par
\small patience — Latin pati, to undergo; the same root gives English patient, passion and compassion\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 321.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la palabra}\par
\small the word — Latin parabola from Greek parabole, a throwing beside; the same Greek word gave English parable, parabola, parley and parliament\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 332.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la parada}\par
\small the stop — from parar, to stop, and Latin parare, to make ready; English prepare, repair, apparatus, parade and parasol are all the same root\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 330.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la pared}\par
\small the wall of a room — Latin paries, the wall of a house rather than of a town; the town wall was murus, which is Spanish muro and English mural, and paries survives in English only as the parietal bone\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 355.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la pareja}\par
\small the couple, the partner --- Latin par, equal; English pair, par, peer, parity and umpire\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 309.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la parte}\par
\small the part, the share — Latin partem from pars; English part, party, partial, particle, partner and portion all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 345.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la Pascua}\par
\small Easter — Latin pascha, from Greek paskha, from Hebrew pesach, the Passover; English kept a spring goddess's name for the feast but the Latin one for paschal\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 357.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la pena}\par
\small sorrow, a shame — Latin poena, a penalty; English pain, penalty and subpoena all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 320.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la persona}\par
\small the person — Latin persona, an actor's mask; English person, personality, persona and impersonate all still wear it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 345.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la piel}\par
\small the skin — Latin pellis, a hide, with the e broken to ie; a pelt is the same hide, and a surplice is a shirt worn over one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 300.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la pierna}\par
\small the leg — Latin perna, a ham; Spanish named the living leg after the butcher's cut\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 314.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la plaza}\par
\small the square — Latin platea from Greek plateia, a broad way; English place, plate, plateau and platypus all mean broad\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 325.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la prima}\par
\small the cousin, feminine --- the primus root you can already see in prima donna and prima facie\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 307.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la primavera, el verano, el otoño, el invierno}\par
\small the four seasons — three straightforward, and one whose MEANING quietly shifted from \textquotedblleft{}spring\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 142.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la prisa}\par
\small the hurry, the rush — Latin pressa, from premere to press; English press, pressure, express, impress, oppress and print are all pressings\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 333.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la puerta}\par
\small door — Latin porta, a gate, and the o that opened into ue\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 279.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la raíz}\par
\small the root — Latin radix, which is also the radish, the radical and the thing you eradicate\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 291.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la rama}\par
\small the branch — Latin ramus; when an argument ramifies, it is growing these\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 291.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la razón}\par
\small reason — Latin ratio, rationem, a reckoning; English ratio, ration and rational are the same word arriving whole\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 321.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la risa}\par
\small the laughter — Latin risus from ridere, to laugh; English took the root only in unkind forms — ridicule, deride, risible\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 315.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la rodilla}\par
\small the knee — Latin rotella, a little wheel, from rota; rotate, rotary and roulette are the same wheel\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 293.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ropa}\par
\small clothes — Germanic raupa, plunder, beside raupjan, to pluck or strip; rob, reave and bereave still take, and robe made the same slide from spoils to garment on its own\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 360.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sal}\par
\small salt — Latin sal, salis; salad, salsa, sauce, sausage and salary are the real family, while salud, saludo and salvo belong together to a whole-and-safe root, and salir to a leaping one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 361.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la salida}\par
\small the way out — from salir, and Latin salire, to jump: a Roman jumped out of a room\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 288.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la salud}\par
\small health — Latin salus, salutem, health and safety and a greeting all at once; English salute, salutary and salubrious keep it, and Spanish saludo is a wish for it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 334.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sangre}\par
\small the blood — Latin sanguinem; sanguine once meant ruddy and cheerful because of it, and consanguinity is shared blood\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 300.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sartén}\par
\small the frying pan — Latin sartago; its written accent is a receipt for where the stress went, and the plural hands it back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 297.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sed}\par
\small the thirst — Latin sitis; Spanish does not say you are thirsty, it says you have thirst, and the difference is the point\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 300.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la semana}\par
\small week — Latin septimana, the set of seven; the same septem gives English September and, down the Germanic road, seven\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 322.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la semilla}\par
\small the seed — Latin seminalia, the things for sowing; a seminar is a seed-bed and disseminate is scattering\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 291.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la silla}\par
\small chair — Latin sella, a seat, from the verb to sit\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 279.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sombra}\par
\small the shade — Latin sub umbra, under the shadow; an umbrella is a little one of these\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 289.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sonrisa}\par
\small a smile — subridere, to laugh slightly: a laugh with the volume turned down\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 282.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la sopa}\par
\small the soup — Germanic suppa, a piece of bread soaked in broth; the bread came first and soup, sop and supper are all it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 297.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la suerte}\par
\small luck — Latin sors, sortem, a token drawn from a jar; English sort, sorcery and consort are all lots being drawn\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 320.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la tarde}\par
\small afternoon (la tarde — feminine; also: late)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 2.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la tarjeta}\par
\small a card — a little targe, from French targe, a small shield, from Frankish targa; English target is the same little shield, and it meant a shield for centuries before anyone shot at it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 357.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la taza}\par
\small the cup — Arabic tassa, from Persian; French tasse and the English demitasse are the same vessel\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 294.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la tía}\par
\small the aunt --- the same Greek root feminine; English aunt comes from a wholly different Latin word, amita\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 307.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la tienda}\par
\small the shop — Latin tendere, to stretch; a shop began as a stretched awning, which is why English tent, extend and tendon are relatives\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 311.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la tierra}\par
\small earth, ground, land — Latin terra, the dry part of the world as against the water; terrain, terrace, subterranean, terrestrial, terra cotta and Mediterranean are the family, and terror is not\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 362.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la toalla}\par
\small a towel — a Frankish word that went into French and came out in two languages\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 287.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la vaca}\par
\small the cow — Latin vacca, unchanged in six letters; vaccine is named after her, because the first one came from a cow\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 296.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la ventana}\par
\small window — a wind-hole, built on the same Latin ventus as viento\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 279.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la verdad}\par
\small the truth — Latin veritas from verus, true; English keeps it in verity, verify and verdict, and in the older sense of very\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 324.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la vez}\par
\small a time, an occasion, a turn — Latin vicem, a turn or change; English vice-president, vicar and vicarious are all standing in someone's place\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 330.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la vida}\par
\small life — Latin vita; English vital, vitamin, revive, survive and viable are all built on it, and the vitamin was named by a chemist who thought it was an amine\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 330.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la víspera}\par
\small the eve, the day before — Latin vespera, evening; English vespers is the evening prayer, Greek hesperos is the evening star, and English west is a cousin of both\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 357.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la voz}\par
\small the voice — Latin vox, vocem; English voice, vocal, vowel, vocation, advocate, evoke and provoke all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 332.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{la vuelta}\par
\small the return — from volver, Latin volvere, to roll: a return is a turning back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 288.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{largo}\par
\small long — Latin largus, abundant and generous; English large is the very same word gone one way, largesse keeps the older sense, and Spanish took it the other way, to long\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 365.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{le}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}to him, to her, to you\textquotedblright{} — a Latin case Spanish kept and English threw away\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 93.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{leer}\par
\small to read — from a Latin verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to gather, to pick out\textquotedblright{}\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 155.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lejos}\par
\small far, far away — Latin laxius, more loosely, from laxus loose; English lax, relax, release and leash come off the same slack rope\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 340.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{levantarse}\par
\small to get up, to stand up — \textquotedblleft{}to raise oneself\textquotedblright{}, built from a participle exactly as sentarse was\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 166.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{libre}\par
\small free — Latin liber meaning unowned, which is a different Latin word from the liber that gave libro; English liberty, liberal and deliver come off this one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 326.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{limpio}\par
\small clean — from limpidus, clear, the word English kept for water and Spanish moved to laundry\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 281.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{listo}\par
\small clever with ser, ready with estar — one word whose meaning is decided by the verb in front of it; the RAE traces it to Gothic lists, cunning\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 326.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{llamo}\par
\small I call (from llamar, to call)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 4.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lleno}\par
\small full — Latin plēnus; plenty, plenary, replenish and complete are the borrowed cousins, full is the inherited one, and comply belongs with filling rather than with folding\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 365.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{llovía / llovió}\par
\small the same rain in two tenses — how a story uses the imperfect for the scene and the preterite for the events\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 167.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{llueve}\par
\small rain refuses the hacer pattern and brings its own verb — and its ll- is the sound change you already met in llamar\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 148.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lo}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{} — a word you have been saying since your fourth chapter, in a job you have not met yet\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 83.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lo cual}\par
\small which — pointing back at a whole clause\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 273.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lo siento}\par
\small I'm sorry — literally \textquotedblleft{}I feel it,\textquotedblright{} a naming of the feeling rather than a claim about yourself\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 137.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{los meses}\par
\small the months — Roman gods and emperors, marching almost unchanged from Latin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 145.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{luego}\par
\small then, next — a word you already own from hasta luego, now doing a second job: joining two events in order\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 167.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes}\par
\small the weekdays (Monday–Friday) — worn-down planet-god names\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 138.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mal}\par
\small badly — the partner bien has been waiting for since the opening pages, in a long form and a short one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 228.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mas}\par
\small but — the literary one, without the accent\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 276.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{más despacio}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}more slowly\textquotedblright{} — the request that makes the last sentence solvable\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 15.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{más que}\par
\small more than\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 269.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{más vale pájaro en mano}\par
\small a bird in the hand — the proverb, and what a proverb is\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 274.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{me}\par
\small me / myself\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 4.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{me llamo}\par
\small my name is (literally \textquotedblleft{}I call myself\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 4.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mediodía, medianoche}\par
\small noon and midnight — both halves still fully alive as ordinary Spanish words, unlike French's worn-down midi/minuit\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 146.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{menos}\par
\small less, fewer, except — Latin minus, the twin of magis; English minus, minor, minimum, minister and diminish are all the small end of it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 324.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mi, tu, su}\par
\small my, your informal, and your formal or his or her — before a singular noun\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 49.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mientras}\par
\small while — Latin dum interim, \textquotedblleft{}for the time between\textquotedblright{}; the inter in it is English interim, interval and international\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 323.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mil gracias}\par
\small a thousand thanks — mille, the same thousand that measures a mile\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 283.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mira}\par
\small look — and the tone shifts\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 272.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mismo}\par
\small same, very, self — Vulgar Latin metipsimus, a piled-up superlative of ipse self; English ipso facto and solipsism keep the ipse\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 345.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mucho}\par
\small much / a lot\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 6.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{mucho gusto}\par
\small pleased to meet you (literally \textquotedblleft{}much pleasure\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 6.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{muy}\par
\small very — not a new word at all, but mucho with its ending bitten off, and the shape tells you what is coming next\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 226.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nada}\par
\small nothing — Latin res nata, \textquotedblleft{}a thing born\textquotedblright{}; the res fell away and the born thing came to mean no thing at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 316.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nadie}\par
\small nobody — Latin nati, \textquotedblleft{}born ones\textquotedblright{}, from homines nati, \textquotedblleft{}people born\textquotedblright{}; the exact twin of nada, which was a thing born\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 317.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{negro, blanco}\par
\small black and white — the two words, and the straight-line Latin history of the first one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 139.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nervioso}\par
\small nervous — Latin nervosus from nervus, a sinew; English nerve, nervous and neuron are the same fibre, and -oso is the -ous you already know\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 326.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ni}\par
\small nor, not even — the joining word for two things that are both absent, and the one place Spanish stacks negatives on purpose\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 234.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ni hablar}\par
\small out of the question — \textquotedblleft{}not even to speak of it\textquotedblright{}, two pieces you already own, and the flattest refusal on the dial\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 298.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no}\par
\small no / not\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 7.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no + verb}\par
\small putting \emph{no} in front of the verb — the whole of Spanish negation\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 267.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no ... nada}\par
\small the double negative — where Spanish stacks what English forbids\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 267.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no entiendo}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}I don't understand\textquotedblright{} — the most useful sentence a beginner owns\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 15.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no hay de qué}\par
\small not at all — the reply to thanks, assembled entirely from words you already have\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 283.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{no sé}\par
\small I do not know — saber is Latin sapere, to taste; knowing began as tasting\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 303.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nos}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}us\textquotedblright{} — the object pronoun that speaks for more than one person\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 88.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nuestro, nuestra}\par
\small our — matching a known masculine or feminine singular noun\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 69.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nuevo}\par
\small new — Latin novus, and English new, which is the cousin rather than the loan\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 281.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{nunca}\par
\small never — Latin numquam, ne plus umquam, \textquotedblleft{}not ever\textquotedblright{}; English never is ne plus ever, the identical compound built out of Germanic parts\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 316.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{o}\par
\small or — one letter, and one rule about what happens when the next word starts with the same sound\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 233.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ocupado}\par
\small busy — Latin occupare, to seize; to be busy is to be seized\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 304.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{oír}\par
\small to hear — the half of listening you do not choose, and a verb that sprouts a y\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 165.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{once — quince}\par
\small 11-15 — five single opaque words, each one a Latin compound worn down until the seam disappeared\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 149.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{os}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}you all\textquotedblright{} as the object — the shortest word in the set, and the one that stops at a border\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 90.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{otra vez}\par
\small again — literally another turn; vez is Latin vicem, a turn taken in rotation\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 303.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{otro}\par
\small another, other — Latin alter, which meant the other of a pair rather than any other at all\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 317.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{para}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{} pointing forward — at a destination, a purpose, a deadline, a person meant to receive something\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 176.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{pasar a mejor vida}\par
\small to pass on — and why the language turns away\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 274.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{pensar}\par
\small to think — at root \textquotedblleft{}to weigh\textquotedblright{}, and a stem-changer that breaks e$\to$ie\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 153.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{perdón}\par
\small the other sorry — \textquotedblleft{}give completely\textquotedblright{} — for fault and for getting past people, where lo siento is for regret\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 137.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{pero}\par
\small but — the first word you need to hold two true things against each other, and the first word of any argument\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 218.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{perro}\par
\small dog — a genuinely unsolved etymology, and the Latin word it pushed out\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 150.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{poco}\par
\small little, few — Latin paucus; English paucity is the noun and few is the same root through Germanic, and you already carry it inside tampoco\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 317.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{poder}\par
\small to be able or can — with the singular present forms puedo, puedes, and puede\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 69.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{poner}\par
\small to put or place — with the singular present forms pongo, pones, and pone\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 71.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}for\textquotedblright{} pointing back or through — at a cause, a route, an exchange; and you have been saying it since your first page\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 177.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por ejemplo}\par
\small for example\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 270.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por favor}\par
\small please (literally \textquotedblleft{}for {[}a{]} favour\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 14.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por lo tanto}\par
\small therefore\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 273.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por supuesto}\par
\small of course — supponere, to place under: it was already under the conversation\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 284.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{por un lado… por otro}\par
\small on one hand… on the other — holding two sources at once\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 277.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{porque}\par
\small because — two tiny words fused into one, and the reason a sequence becomes a story\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 167.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{preguntar}\par
\small to ask (a question) — and the reason English's one \textquotedblleft{}ask\textquotedblright{} becomes two Spanish verbs\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 160.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{primero · segundo · tercero}\par
\small first, second, third — the counting words for order rather than amount, and the story inside the second one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 262.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{problema}\par
\small problem\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 268.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{profesor}\par
\small teacher — and the one place Spanish drops the \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{} that English insists on\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 51.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{propio}\par
\small one's own — Latin proprius, belonging to the individual; English proper, property and appropriate all began as words about owning\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 350.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{próximo}\par
\small next, nearest — Latin proximus, nearest, the superlative of prope near; English proximity, approximate, approach and reproach come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 343.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{puede ser}\par
\small could be — two words you already own, standing side by side and meaning less together than either does alone\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 298.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{pues}\par
\small well, then, since — Latin post, after; the same post is inside despues, and English keeps it raw in post-, posterior and postpone\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 329.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{qué}\par
\small what? (a new question word for verbs you already know)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 36.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{querer}\par
\small to want — with the singular present forms quiero, quieres, and quiere\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 69.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{quién}\par
\small who — the asking word Spanish keeps for people, and the reason qué has never had to do that job\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 232.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{quién}\par
\small who? — one tiny people-question before the writing marks are explained\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 5.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{quizás}\par
\small maybe, perhaps\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 271.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{regular}\par
\small so-so / not great (also \textquotedblleft{}más o menos\textquotedblright{})\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 9.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{rojo}\par
\small red — a cousin of French rouge and English red, but by a different branch of the same very old family\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 139.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sábado, domingo}\par
\small the weekend (Saturday, Sunday) — where religion overwrote astronomy\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 138.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{salir}\par
\small to leave or go out — with the singular present forms salgo, sales, and sale\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 72.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{salvo}\par
\small except, safe — Latin salvus, unharmed; English salvage, salvation, salvo, salve and safe itself all come off it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 329.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sano}\par
\small healthy — Latin sanus, sound in body and mind; English sane, sanity, insane, sanitary and sanatorium are the same word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 327.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{se llama}\par
\small he/she calls himself; you (formal) call yourself\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 6.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{según}\par
\small according to — marking whose claim it is\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 277.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{seguro}\par
\small sure — se- without plus cura, care: free from care, and so reliable\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 284.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez}\par
\small the numbers 6–10 and the old counting hidden in month names\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 47.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{señor}\par
\small sir, Mr — Latin senior, older; respect built out of age\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 305.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{señora}\par
\small madam, Mrs — the feminine of senor, on the same Latin senior\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 305.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sentarse}\par
\small to sit down — literally \textquotedblleft{}to seat oneself\textquotedblright{}, the reflexive that lands the action back on you\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 166.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ser}\par
\small to be — the verb used here to identify someone or say what someone is\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 48.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ser un quijote}\par
\small to be a Quixote — an allusion working as a word\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 274.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ser vs estar}\par
\small identify with ser; describe a current state or location with estar\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 48.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sí}\par
\small yes\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 7.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sí que}\par
\small the emphatic yes — contradicting something unsaid\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 275.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sí, claro}\par
\small yeah, right\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 272.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{siempre}\par
\small always — Latin semper, kept almost whole; sempiternal is semper plus aeternus, everlasting said twice\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 316.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sin duda}\par
\small no doubt — duda is dubitare, and behind that duo, two: to doubt is to be caught between a pair of answers\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 298.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sin embargo}\par
\small however, nevertheless\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 270.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sino}\par
\small but rather — si plus no, if not; the negative that corrects a negative, and both halves are words you already have\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 329.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{siquiera}\par
\small even, at least — two words you already have, si and quiera, welded into one; ni siquiera is not even\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 324.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{solo}\par
\small alone, and also only — Latin solus; the accent that once separated the two meanings was abolished in 2010, so five letters now do both jobs\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 326.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{soy de…}\par
\small I am from… — use ser with de to state origin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 48.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{sucio}\par
\small dirty — from sucidus, greasy with its own juice, said first of unwashed wool\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 281.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{supongo que}\par
\small I suppose that\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 271.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tal}\par
\small such, such a — Latin talis, of that kind; English keeps it in retaliate, to give back the like, and in the lawyers' lex talionis\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 329.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tal vez}\par
\small maybe — literally \textquotedblleft{}such a turn\textquotedblright{}, from vicem, a turn or a change; vice versa is the turn turned round\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 298.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{también}\par
\small also — and you have been holding half of it since the first chapter of this book\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 219.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tampoco}\par
\small neither — the same tan, a different second half, and the word that lets you agree with a no\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 220.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{te quiero}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} as the object — and the sentence it makes, which is the one people actually need\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 85.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{temprano}\par
\small early — Latin temporanus, in good time, built on tempus; English temporary, tempo and contemporary share the root, and so does el tiempo\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 322.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tener}\par
\small to have — a common verb with two visible changes\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 47.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tener gracia}\par
\small to be funny — and a word that does not translate\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 274.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tengo · hago · digo}\par
\small comparing the three learned yo forms that end in -go\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 70.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{todavía}\par
\small still, yet — literally toda vía, \textquotedblleft{}all the road\textquotedblright{}; the via in it is English via, viaduct, deviate and obvious\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 322.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{todo}\par
\small all, everything — Latin totus; English total is the same word, and Portuguese tudo is its sibling down a parallel road\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 316.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tomar}\par
\small to take (and, across Latin America, to drink) — an everyday word with no settled origin\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 159.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tomar el pelo}\par
\small to pull someone's leg (lit. to take the hair)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 272.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{trabajar}\par
\small to work (a second -ar verb — same pattern)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 20.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{traer}\par
\small to bring — Latin's word for dragging, and a verb with a direction built into it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 168.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tranquilo}\par
\small calm — Latin tranquillus, the word for a sea with no wind on it\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 304.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{triste}\par
\small sad — Latin tristis, which also meant harsh and grim before it softened\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 304.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tú / usted}\par
\small two of the three words Spanish uses to one person — and the one English quietly retired\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 5.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{tú o usted}\par
\small the choice English lost — and the surprise that usted takes he/she verb forms\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 5.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco}\par
\small the numbers 1–5\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 47.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{valiente}\par
\small brave — the old present participle of valer, from Latin valere, to be strong or be worth; English valiant, valour, value and valid are the same root\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 326.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{varios}\par
\small several — Latin varius, speckled, of mixed colours; English various, variety and variegated all start from a spotted hide\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 351.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{veinte}\par
\small twenty — the ceiling of the teens, and a word that was worn but never fused\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 149.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{venir}\par
\small to come — with the singular present forms vengo, vienes, and viene\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 73.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ver}\par
\small to see — veo, ves, ve\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 108.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{verde}\par
\small green — from a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to flourish,\textquotedblright{} and a cousin of verdant but not of English green\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 151.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{viejo}\par
\small old — from vetulus, \textquotedblleft{}little old one\textquotedblright{}, the affectionate form rather than the plain one\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 281.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{viví}\par
\small the regular singular -ir preterite — viví, viviste, vivió\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 104.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{vivir}\par
\small to live — your first -ir verb, and a family that asks you to learn nothing new\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 35.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{vos}\par
\small \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} across a large part of the Spanish-speaking world — to recognise, not to say\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 5.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{voy a + infinitive}\par
\small I am going to… — the near future with ir, a, and a known infinitive\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 49.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{y / ¿y tú?}\par
\small and / and you? — a tiny connector that hands the conversation back\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 9.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{ya}\par
\small already, now — Latin iam; English borrowed it without knowing, in the déjà of déjà vu\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 323.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿cómo está usted?}\par
\small how are you? — assemble the formal question from cómo, estar, and usted\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 8.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿cómo se dice?}\par
\small the single most useful sentence a learner owns — and it is this chapter's grammar, doing exactly what the chapter said\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 183.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿cómo se llama usted?}\par
\small what's your name? (formal)\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 6.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿Cuántos años tienes?}\par
\small how old are you? — literally, how many years do you have?\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 47.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿dónde está?}\par
\small where is it?\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 268.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿Hablas español?}\par
\small the yes-or-no question — and why Spanish barely has to do anything\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 267.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿qué significa?}\par
\small what does it mean — significar is Latin significare, to make a sign\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 303.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip

\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{\linewidth}
\raggedright
\textbf{¿verdad?}\par
\small the tag question — asking someone to agree\par
\footnotesize Introduced in Chapter 267.
\end{minipage}\par\medskip
